title: Thread Pool Pattern
oneLiner: Reuses a fixed crew of worker threads to run many tasks, instead of spawning and destroying a thread for every single one.

hero.name: The Crew
hero.catchphrase: Same crew, every job. No hiring a new worker for every task.
hero.power: Maintains a fixed set of worker threads pulling from a shared task queue, avoiding the cost of spawning a new thread per task.
hero.weakness: Size the crew wrong and everything suffers — too small starves under load, too large wastes memory and burns time on context switching.
hero.origin: The Crew appeared after a web server spawned a brand-new OS thread for every incoming request and fell over under load, spending more time creating and destroying threads than actually serving requests.

story.problem: Every incoming HTTP request spawns a brand-new OS thread. Under a traffic spike, thread creation and teardown overhead alone consumes more CPU than actually handling requests, and the server falls over.
story.solution: The Crew pre-creates a fixed pool of 20 worker threads at startup. Incoming requests are placed on a shared queue; idle workers pull the next request the instant they're free.
story.result: Thread creation happens exactly 20 times, at startup — never again. The server handles traffic spikes by queueing, not by exploding its thread count.

before: A new thread is created and destroyed for every task
Thread creation overhead dominates under heavy load
Thread count grows unbounded with incoming traffic
after: A fixed set of threads is created exactly once
Thread creation overhead is paid only at startup
Thread count stays capped no matter how much traffic arrives

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A server monitor shows CPU usage spiking not from request handling, but from constant thread creation and teardown.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We're spending more CPU spinning up and tearing down threads than actually serving requests. This traffic spike is killing us.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Crew appears — twenty workers standing ready, no hiring needed for the next job.
panels.speaker: The Crew
panels.dialogue: Stop hiring a new worker for every task. Keep the same crew on hand — we'll pull the next job the instant we're free.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Twenty pre-created worker threads pull tasks from a shared queue. New requests just get queued, never spawn a thread.
panels.speaker: The Crew
panels.dialogue: We were created once, at startup. Every request after that just waits in line for the next free worker — no new threads, ever.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The same traffic spike now just grows the queue briefly, with thread count never moving.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Thread count stays flat at 20 no matter what traffic throws at us. Requests queue gracefully instead of crashing the server.

useWhen: You process many short-lived tasks and thread creation/teardown overhead is a measurable cost.
You need to cap concurrent resource usage (threads, memory) under unpredictable load.
Tasks are roughly independent and can be processed in any order by any available worker.
avoidWhen: Task volume is low enough that thread creation overhead was never actually a bottleneck.
Tasks are long-running or blocking in ways that would starve the fixed-size pool — you'd need a much larger pool or a different model entirely.
Your runtime already provides a well-tuned thread/worker pool (many frameworks and languages do) — building your own duplicates that work.
commonMistakes: Sizing the pool too small, causing tasks to queue and starve under load even though CPU capacity exists.
Sizing the pool too large, wasting memory and causing excessive context-switching overhead that hurts throughput.
Submitting long-blocking tasks to a pool sized for short, fast tasks, starving the rest of the queue.
Not monitoring queue depth, missing the early warning signs of a pool that's undersized for current load.
explanation.realWorldExample: Web server worker pools (Node.js's libuv thread pool, Java's `ExecutorService`, most HTTP server frameworks), and database connection pools' 'worker' counterparts, are all Thread Pool in practice.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from Object Pool?

conversation.speaker: The Crew
conversation.message: Same core idea — reuse instead of recreate — applied specifically to threads instead of arbitrary objects. I manage WORKERS that pull TASKS from a queue; Object Pool manages reusable objects that get borrowed and returned directly.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How do I pick the right crew size?

conversation.speaker: The Crew
conversation.message: That's the real art. Too few, and tasks queue up and starve even with spare CPU capacity. Too many, and you're burning memory and context-switch time on workers that mostly wait around. Measure, don't guess.

codeBattle.scenario: Your image-resizing API spawns a new OS thread for every incoming resize request, and under a traffic spike the server spends most of its CPU just creating and destroying threads instead of resizing images.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Crew pre-creates a fixed set of worker threads once, so resize requests queue and get processed without ever paying thread-creation cost per request.

quiz.question: What does Thread Pool primarily save?
options: The overhead of creating and destroying a thread for every task
The memory used by task data itself
quiz.answer: The overhead of creating and destroying a thread for every task
quiz.explanation: Thread Pool's entire value is amortizing thread creation cost across many reused workers instead of paying it per task.

quiz.question: What happens when more tasks arrive than there are available worker threads?
options: Tasks wait in a queue until a worker becomes free
New threads are spawned automatically without limit
The extra tasks are silently dropped
quiz.answer: Tasks wait in a queue until a worker becomes free
quiz.explanation: Queueing excess tasks, rather than spawning unlimited threads, is exactly what keeps thread count capped and predictable.

quiz.question: What's the risk of sizing a Thread Pool too small?
options: Tasks queue up and starve even when there's spare CPU capacity available
It becomes impossible to submit any tasks at all
quiz.answer: Tasks queue up and starve even when there's spare CPU capacity available
quiz.explanation: An undersized pool can bottleneck throughput even when the machine has room to do more concurrent work.

quiz.question: How does Thread Pool differ from Object Pool?
options: Thread Pool manages reusable worker threads pulling tasks from a queue; Object Pool manages reusable objects borrowed and returned directly
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Object Pool can only be used with threads
Thread Pool requires a database connection to function
quiz.answer: Thread Pool manages reusable worker threads pulling tasks from a queue; Object Pool manages reusable objects borrowed and returned directly
quiz.explanation: Both apply the same 'reuse instead of recreate' idea, but to different kinds of expensive resources.
